primitives.name: Bellman-Closed Statistics
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Theorem 4.3 (Bellman-closedness characterization): the only finite sets of statistics of this form that are Bellman closed are those whose linear span equals the span of moment functionals {μ ↦ E_{Z∼μ}[Z^l] | l=0,...,L} for some L ≤ K.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'L': 'maximum moment order', 'K': 'number of statistics', 's(μ)': 'vector of statistics of μ'}
primitives.assumptions: Linear span equality with moment functionals, finite-dimensional space
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure when moment-based statistics fail to capture full distributional structure

primitives.name: Expectile-Based Algorithm
primitives.verbatim_quote: **EDRL (expectile DRL):** learn K expectiles of the return distribution with asymmetric-least-squares loss, using a sample-based imputation strategy (SciPy root-finding/optimization per update, Eq 7–8) to construct Bellman targets consistent with learned expectiles.

primitives.assumptions: Asymmetric least squares loss, solvable root-finding per update

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that any distributional reinforcement learning algorithm can be decomposed into two components: a statistical estimator that extracts summary statistics from the return distribution, and an imputation strategy that reconstructs a full distribution from these statistics. This duality allows for systematic analysis of algorithmic behavior. Bellman-closedness arises when the set of statistics used is such that Bellman updates preserve them exactly—this occurs precisely when their linear span matches that of moment functionals up to some order L. Algorithms like C51 and QR-DQN do not satisfy this condition, meaning they approximate rather than exactly compute the return distribution. EDRL/ER-DQN sidesteps this by learning expectiles directly, which are more expressive than quantiles but still allow for tractable imputation. The failure mode lies in imputation inconsistency—when the reconstructed distribution does not match the learned statistics, especially in terms of mean preservation. This leads to misranking of actions in policy selection, as seen in the two-action choice example where C51 and QR-DQN incorrectly select suboptimal stakes due to mean-inconsistent critics.
